Hi everyone,

I would appreciate some guidance before preparing a Mathlib4 PR.

I have been working on a Lean 4 formalization of spectral graph theory results around the graph Laplacian. The project includes:

  • A full formal proof of a Cheeger-type lower bound for λ₂ (algebraic connectivity)
  • Several spectral identities involving adjacency and Laplacian matrices
  • A trace identity relating triangles to trace(A³)
  • A quadratic form identity: xᵀ L x = ∑_{edges} (x_u - x_v)²
  • Some auxiliary combinatorial lemmas (edge ↔ directed representations, fiber counting, etc.)

The main results are part of a research project, but I would like to extract the general-purpose lemmas and contribute them to Mathlib.

Before preparing a PR, I have a few questions:

  1. Which parts would be considered appropriate for Mathlib?
    (e.g. spectral identities, Laplacian trace results, combinatorial counting lemmas)

  2. Are there existing results in Mathlib4 that overlap with:

    • trace(A³) and triangle counting
    • Laplacian quadratic form identities
    • regular graph spectral decompositions

  3. Is there a preferred location/module for such results?
    (linear algebra? combinatorics? spectral graph theory is still somewhat spread out)

  4. Would it be better to split contributions into several small PRs (e.g. one for trace identities, one for combinatorial lemmas)?

I’m happy to adapt everything to Mathlib style and generalize statements where appropriate.

Thanks a lot for your guidance!

Laura Monk said :

Hi! How exciting, I have been having similar goals, see here: https://lauramonk.github.io/FriedmanStrongConv/

Thanks very much — this is really helpful, and very relevant to what I’m trying to do.

My current project is a Lean 4 formalization around Laplacian / adjacency spectral identities, Cheeger-type bounds, and some graph-structural inequalities. I’m trying to separate the reusable library lemmas from the paper-specific results before preparing any Mathlib PRs.

Your work looks closely related in spirit, especially on the spectral graph side, so I’ll read it carefully. If you have any advice on what kinds of graph spectral lemmas were easiest/hardest to upstream into Mathlib, I’d be very interested.

Thanks again!

So far nothing has been made in Lean let alone added to Mathlib ;) here are a few personal goals on the edge of the project:

  • Cheeger inequalities
  • the Alon Boppanna bound
  • defining the adjacency operator for infinite graphs
  • defining the universal cover
  • computing the spectrum of the infinite regular tree
    The rest (strong convergence and Friedman's theorem) are a more "sexy" goal long term but I actually would really like all of these to be represented in Mathlib in the long run

Snir Broshi said :

#36335

Thanks — this is very helpful.

I also noticed PR #36335, which already adds the Hermitian infrastructure for adj/deg/lap matrices. That seems like exactly the right base layer.

What I currently have goes a bit further up the stack: quadratic-form identities for the Laplacian, trace/triangle identities, and some spectral lemmas for regular graphs / lifted edge functions. So I think the right approach would be to avoid duplicating #36335 and instead extract only the reusable results that build on top of it.

If that sounds reasonable, I’d be happy to prepare a small list of candidate lemmas before opening any PR.

I'm interested in formalizing spectral graph theory as well, for now some basic results that are lacking is the spectrum of a complete graph (I have a half baked proof with a few sorries on my local machine but I haven't had the time to clean it up and contribute it), and the fact that (nontrivial) strongly regular graphs have 3 distinct eigenvalues.
Interacting with the eigenvalues API is difficult at the moment and I wonder what we can do to make it easier.

Great to see the interest! Following up on my earlier message —
the formalization is now complete and sorry-free.

Repo: https://github.com/zeekmartin/topostability-lean4

@Rida Hamadani — completely agree on the eigenvalue API difficulty.
The hardest part in our formalization was exactly this: composing
Matrix.IsHermitian.spectral_theorem, eigenvectorUnitary, and
eigenvalues₀_antitone to get usable spectral bounds.

What we ended up proving that might help:

  • algebraicConnectivity_pos: λ₂ > 0 for connected graphs
  • algebraicConnectivity_le_rayleigh: Rayleigh quotient bound
  • lambda2_upper_bound_regular: uses full spectral decomposition P·Λ·P*

Happy to do a diff with anyone working on similar results to avoid
duplication before any Mathlib PR. The sweep-cut / Cheeger chain
(discrete_coarea, cheeger_inequality) is probably the most
self-contained contribution candidate.

@Laura Monk — your Cheeger goal is directly covered. Would love to
compare approaches.
Hey, could you please clarify your use of LLMs? Specifically, are you using an LLM to communicate on Zulip, and are your proofs autoformalized?

Snir Broshi said :

Hey, could you please clarify your use of LLMs? Specifically, are you using an LLM to communicate on Zulip, and are your proofs autoformalized?

Snir — fair question, and I'll be transparent.

Yes, I used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant throughout the formalization. Concretely: I drove the mathematical strategy, the framework and proof structure, Claude helped with Lean 4 syntax, tactic selection, and Mathlib API lookup. All proofs were iterated in a live Codespace with lake build as the ground truth — no autoformalization from paper text.

The theorems are sorry-free and depend only on: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound (verified via #print axioms for each main theorem)

For Zulip communication: I'm writing the messages myself, with some help drafting from Claude when my English needs polish.

I think this is worth being upfront about. The mathematical content and proof strategy are mine; the LLM accelerated the Lean implementation significantly. Happy to discuss the methodology further if useful for the community.

I come from a software engineering background and I treat formal verification and security seriously — every claim is backed by a clean lake build, not just plausibility.

David MARTIN said:

no autoformalization from paper text.

Are you saying that your commit messages are incorrectly mentioning they are formalizing a paper?

Snir Broshi said :

David MARTIN said:

no autoformalization from paper text.

Are you saying that your commit messages are incorrectly mentioning they are formalizing a paper?

@Snir Broshi

The paper (Paper 13 - Triangle-connectivity graphs and a spectral dominance conjecture for regular graphs) was written first — the conjecture τ(G) ≤ λ₂(G) is stated and argued informally there. The Lean 4 formalization came after, so the commit messages are accurate: they formalize a result already in the paper, now on Zenodo (zenodo.org/records/18999097) and under review at Journal of Graph Theory.

For context on where this came from: the conjecture emerged from the Topostability framework (cognitive-engineering.dev), which classifies edges in complex networks by local triangle count — tri(e).

A related paper was just accepted at Trusts & Trustees (Oxford University Press), and the framework has been validated across oncology, ecology, and neural circuits.

Early in the development, I had an exchange with Rafael Sorkin (Perimeter Institute, father of causal set theory) whose remark on discrete relational structure influenced how I thought about the tri(e) metric. The conjecture felt inevitable once the applied results were in — and Lean 4 was the right way to close it properly.

Snir Broshi said :

So you are autoformalizing a paper?

No — autoformalization would mean feeding the paper to an LLM and getting Lean code out automatically. That's not what happened here. The proof structure, lemma decomposition, and overall architecture were designed by hand. LLM assistance was used for tactic search in some steps, but the Lean kernel verified the result independently.

The paper is on Zenodo if you want to check the mathematical argument: zenodo.org/records/18999097. Happy to discuss any specific objections there.
